title: Arithmetic
tagline: Percentages, interest, P&L, ratios, mixtures, speed — the bulk of QA marks.

subsections.title: Simplification — Core Identities
subsections.trick: Spot (a+b)² − (a−b)² = 4ab instantly — examiners hide this to force long multiplication. Also memorise a³±b³ factorisations cold; they show up inside “simplify the fraction” questions constantly.

subsections.title: Percentages
subsections.trick: Convert every percentage question into a fraction first (12.5% = 1/8, 16.67% = 1/6, 33.33% = 1/3, 37.5% = 3/8) — fraction arithmetic is faster than decimal arithmetic under time pressure.

formulas.label: ‘A is r% more/less than B’ → B vs A
formulas.latex: B \text{ is } \dfrac{100r}{100 \pm r}\% \text{ less/more than } A

subsections.title: Simple & Compound Interest
subsections.trick: For CI over 2–3 years, don’t expand the binomial — use the CI−SI shortcut formulas directly. For ‘amounts to X times in T years’ questions, decide SI vs CI first: SI scales linearly with time, CI does not.

subsections.title: Profit, Loss & Discount
subsections.trick: ‘Same SP, one at +X% one at −X%’ is always a net loss of X²/100 percent — never a wash. Keep CP as the base for profit% and MP as the base for discount% — mixing the two bases is the #1 error here.

subsections.title: Ratio & Proportion
subsections.trick: Componendo–Dividendo saves a full page of algebra on ‘find x given a ratio equation’ questions — recognise the a/b = c/d pattern immediately and jump straight to (c).

subsections.title: Alligation, Mixtures & Means
subsections.trick: Draw the alligation cross every time — it turns a two-line weighted average calculation into a single ratio read-off. Remember AM ≥ GM ≥ HM always, with equality only when all values are equal.

subsections.title: Time, Speed & Distance
subsections.trick: Constant distance → average speed is the Harmonic Mean of the two speeds; constant time → it's the Arithmetic Mean. Mixing these up is the single most common TSD error. For boats: add for downstream, subtract for upstream — always solve for B and R from D and U, not the other way round.
